ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Spinning Cylinder Adithya has a solid cylinder of mass $M=10 \mathrm{~kg}$, radius $R=0.08 \mathrm{~m}$, and height $H=0.20 \mathrm{~m}$. He is running a test in a chamber on Earth over a distance of $d=200 \mathrm{~m}$ as shown below. Assume that the physical length of the chamber is much greater than $d$ (i.e. the chamber extends far to the left and right of the testing area). The chamber is filled with an ideal fluid with uniform density $\rho=700 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$. Adithya's cylinder is launched with linear velocity $v=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and spins counterclockwise with angular velocity $\omega$. Adithya notices that the cylinder continues on a horizontal path until the end of the chamber. Find the angular velocity $\omega$. Do not neglect forces due to fluid pressure differences. Note that the diagram presents a side view of the chamber (i.e. gravity is oriented downwards with respect to the diagram).
<image_1>

Assume the following about the setup and the ideal fluid:

- fluid flow is steady in the frame of the center of mass of the cylinder
- the ideal fluid is incompressible, irrotational, and has zero viscosity
- the angular velocity of the cylinder is approximately constant during its subsequent motion

Hint: For a uniform cylinder of radius $R$ rotating counterclockwise at angular velocity $\omega$ situated in an ideal fluid with flow velocity $u$ to the right far away from the cylinder, the velocity potential $\Phi$ is given by

$$
\Phi(r, \theta)=u r \cos \theta+u \frac{R^{2}}{r} \cos \theta+\frac{\Gamma \theta}{2 \pi}
$$

where $(r, \theta)$ is the polar coordinate system with origin at the center of the cylinder. $\Gamma$ is the circulation and is equal to $2 \pi R^{2} \omega$. The fluid velocity is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}=\nabla \Phi=\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial r} \hat{\mathbf{r}}+\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \theta} \hat{\theta}
$$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure is a side-view schematic of a long horizontal chamber, with horizontal boundaries above and below the chamber and a light gray region inside. On the left there is a cylinder with a gray circular cross-section; beside the cylinder is a straight arrow pointing right labeled 10 m/s, indicating that the cylinder moves to the right along the horizontal dashed line; above the cylinder there is a curved arrow labeled ω, whose direction is counterclockwise. Below, a bidirectional arrow marks the test distance 200 m. The problem text states that gravity is downward relative to the figure. Reasoning: In the center-of-mass frame of the cylinder, take the far-field flow speed as u = 10 m/s, and choose the sign according to the problem/method convention so that a right-moving cylinder rotating counterclockwise produces an upward Magnus lift. From the given potential function Φ = u r cosθ + u R^2 cosθ/r + Γθ/(2π), the velocity components are v_r = u(1 - R^2/r^2)cosθ and v_θ = -u(1 + R^2/r^2)sinθ + Γ/(2πr). On the cylinder surface r = R, v_r = 0 and v_θ = -2u sinθ + Γ/(2πR). Using the Bernoulli equation p + (1/2)ρv^2 + ρgy = constant, and y = R sinθ, obtain the surface pressure. Integrating the vertical component of pressure over the cylinder side area element dA = RH dθ, F_y = -∫ p sinθ RH dθ. The hydrostatic pressure part gives upward buoyancy F_b = ρgπR^2H; the circulation-translation cross term in the velocity squared gives the upward Magnus force F_M = ρuΓH; the vertical integrals of the other symmetric terms are zero. The cylinder maintains a horizontal path, and its vertical acceleration is zero, so ρgπR^2H + ρuΓH = Mg. Substituting Γ = 2πR^2ω gives ω = (Mg - ρgπR^2H)/(ρuH·2πR^2). Numerical substitution M = 10 kg, ρ = 700 kg/m^3, R = 0.08 m, H = 0.20 m, u = 10 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s^2: Mg - ρgπR^2H ≈ 98 - 700·9.8·π·(0.08)^2·0.20 ≈ 70.4 N; ρuH·2πR^2 ≈ 700·10·0.20·2π·(0.08)^2 ≈ 56.3. Therefore ω ≈ 70.4/56.3 ≈ 1.25 rad/s.

method.method_draft: Use the supplied velocity potential directly. First read the diagram as a side view: the cylinder starts at the left, moves horizontally to the right along the dashed line at 10 m/s, spins counterclockwise, and gravity is downward in the page. In the cylinder center-of-mass frame, take the far-field fluid speed magnitude as u = 10 m/s, with sign chosen consistently with the given potential/circulation convention. From the text, use R = 0.08 m, H = 0.20 m, M = 10 kg, rho = 700 kg/m^3, and Gamma = 2 pi R^2 omega. Differentiate the potential to get v_r and v_theta, evaluate on r = R so v_r = 0 and v_theta contains the translational-flow term plus Gamma/(2 pi R). Apply Bernoulli including gravitational potential, p + 1/2 rho v^2 + rho g y = constant, to obtain the pressure around the cylinder surface. Integrate the pressure force over the cylindrical side surface in the vertical direction. The hydrostatic part gives buoyancy rho g pi R^2 H upward, and the dynamic circulation part gives the Magnus lift rho u Gamma H upward for the counterclockwise spin/rightward motion. Since the image/text state the path remains horizontal, impose zero vertical acceleration: rho g pi R^2 H + rho u Gamma H = Mg. Substitute Gamma = 2 pi R^2 omega and solve for omega, giving approximately 1.25 rad/s.

raw_record.original_question:
Spinning Cylinder Adithya has a solid cylinder of mass $M=10 \mathrm{~kg}$, radius $R=0.08 \mathrm{~m}$, and height $H=0.20 \mathrm{~m}$. He is running a test in a chamber on Earth over a distance of $d=200 \mathrm{~m}$ as shown below. Assume that the physical length of the chamber is much greater than $d$ (i.e. the chamber extends far to the left and right of the testing area). The chamber is filled with an ideal fluid with uniform density $\rho=700 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$. Adithya's cylinder is launched with linear velocity $v=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and spins counterclockwise with angular velocity $\omega$. Adithya notices that the cylinder continues on a horizontal path until the end of the chamber. Find the angular velocity $\omega$ in $\mathrm{rad/s}$. Do not neglect forces due to fluid pressure differences. Note that the diagram presents a side view of the chamber (i.e. gravity is oriented downwards with respect to the diagram).

Assume the following about the setup and the ideal fluid:

- fluid flow is steady in the frame of the center of mass of the cylinder
- the ideal fluid is incompressible, irrotational, and has zero viscosity
- the angular velocity of the cylinder is approximately constant during its subsequent motion

Hint: For a uniform cylinder of radius $R$ rotating counterclockwise at angular velocity $\omega$ situated in an ideal fluid with flow velocity $u$ to the right far away from the cylinder, the velocity potential $\Phi$ is given by

$$
\Phi(r, \theta)=u r \cos \theta+u \frac{R^{2}}{r} \cos \theta+\frac{\Gamma \theta}{2 \pi}
$$

where $(r, \theta)$ is the polar coordinate system with origin at the center of the cylinder. $\Gamma$ is the circulation and is equal to $2 \pi R^{2} \omega$. The fluid velocity is given by

$$
\mathbf{v}=\nabla \Phi=\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial r} \hat{\mathbf{r}}+\frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \theta} \hat{\theta}
$$
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure is a side-view schematic of a long horizontal chamber, with horizontal boundaries above and below the chamber and a light gray region inside. On the left there is a cylinder with a gray circular cross-section; beside the cylinder is a straight arrow pointing right labeled 10 m/s, indicating that the cylinder moves to the right along the horizontal dashed line; above the cylinder there is a curved arrow labeled ω, whose direction is counterclockwise. Below, a bidirectional arrow marks the test distance 200 m. The problem text states that gravity is downward relative to the figure. Reasoning: In the center-of-mass frame of the cylinder, take the far-field flow speed as u = 10 m/s, and choose the sign according to the problem/method convention so that a right-moving cylinder rotating counterclockwise produces an upward Magnus lift. From the given potential function Φ = u r cosθ + u R^2 cosθ/r + Γθ/(2π), the velocity components are v_r = u(1 - R^2/r^2)cosθ and v_θ = -u(1 + R^2/r^2)sinθ + Γ/(2πr). On the cylinder surface r = R, v_r = 0 and v_θ = -2u sinθ + Γ/(2πR). Using the Bernoulli equation p + (1/2)ρv^2 + ρgy = constant, and y = R sinθ, obtain the surface pressure. Integrating the vertical component of pressure over the cylinder side area element dA = RH dθ, F_y = -∫ p sinθ RH dθ. The hydrostatic pressure part gives upward buoyancy F_b = ρgπR^2H; the circulation-translation cross term in the velocity squared gives the upward Magnus force F_M = ρuΓH; the vertical integrals of the other symmetric terms are zero. The cylinder maintains a horizontal path, and its vertical acceleration is zero, so ρgπR^2H + ρuΓH = Mg. Substituting Γ = 2πR^2ω gives ω = (Mg - ρgπR^2H)/(ρuH·2πR^2). Numerical substitution M = 10 kg, ρ = 700 kg/m^3, R = 0.08 m, H = 0.20 m, u = 10 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s^2: Mg - ρgπR^2H ≈ 98 - 700·9.8·π·(0.08)^2·0.20 ≈ 70.4 N; ρuH·2πR^2 ≈ 700·10·0.20·2π·(0.08)^2 ≈ 56.3. Therefore ω ≈ 70.4/56.3 ≈ 1.25 rad/s.
